subtitle: The whole proverb, and five shades of the Konjunktiv II
words.intro: About a million German families have an allotment. Its hedge has a legal height, its lawn a legal share of the plot, and its gnomes a long and contested history. Neighbours here have talked in proverbs for generations. It’s how to fight without saying anything.

grammar[0].blocks[1].root.no.example: Viele Köche, kein Brei · im Glashaus sitzen
grammar[0].fact: Germans often give only the first half and leave you to finish: *Wer A sagt …*, *Wer im Glashaus sitzt …*. If you know the second half, you’re in. A proverb used in full, slowly, by someone who has never used it before will produce the silence you’ve just read.

grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Five shades
grammar[1].blocks[1].rows[0][1]: Um ein Haar *wäre* ich gestürzt. (I didn’t fall)
grammar[1].fact: You know the form. These are its uses: what nearly happened, what you regret, what you ask politely. *Um ein Haar wäre ich gefallen* tells you I didn’t fall. And at C2, it’s also how Germans say *I know*: *Das hätte ich dir gleich sagen können*.

document.intro: A real notice from an allotment club: the water’s coming back on. It’s all here: the red letters, three exclamation marks and the club’s monopoly on water meters. Notice *aller Voraussicht nach*, a very careful way of saying *probably*.
document.fact: Some of the commas here are missing, and *ihre* has lost its capital. You may find you can see that now. In the club it doesn’t matter at all. They all know what happens if your meter isn’t from the club.

reading.intro: Frau Huber has taken over a small plot in the Kolonie Abendruh. Her new neighbour, Herr Kolb, the driving examiner, is now retired. His hedge is 1.31 metres high. The rules say 1.25. It is a warm Sunday. Max is holding the ladder, and he has asked what the problem is.
reading.fact: The Federal Allotment Act really does set out the use of these plots, and the local rules go further: about a third for fruit and vegetables, hedges to a set height, and quiet hours at midday. Waiting lists in big cities run to years. Your gnome is a private matter, but your neighbour may have a view.
